definition: The bitter lesson is the observation in artificial intelligence that, in the long run, general approaches that scale with available computational power tend to outperform ones based on domain-specific understanding because they are better at taking advantage of the falling cost of computation over time.
details: The principle was proposed and named in a 2019 essay by Richard Sutton and is now widely accepted.

explainer.lead: The bitter lesson is a rule of thumb for building AI: as computers get cheaper and faster, broad methods that can use more computation often beat systems packed with specialist knowledge. It matters because it changes where researchers place their bets—on approaches that keep improving with scale rather than on clever shortcuts that eventually stop helping.

tiers.eli5: Instead of hand-crafting clever shortcuts, just give a simple learner more practice time and cheap horsepower, and it usually wins.
tiers.practitioner: Engineers use it to justify investing in scale and general architectures over bespoke feature engineering, but a pitfall is ignoring cases where data or compute is scarce.
tiers.paperLevel: Proposed and named in a 2019 essay by Richard Sutton, it states that general approaches scaling with available computational power tend to outperform domain-specific ones as computation gets cheaper; it is an observation, not a theorem.

explainer.example: Imagine two chess programs: one relies on a large collection of hand-written chess rules, while the other uses a general search method. The rule-based program may be stronger when computation is limited, but the general program can use increasingly cheap computation to search more possibilities and eventually perform better.
explainer.intuition: Human-written rules can give an AI system an early advantage, but they are difficult to expand indefinitely. General methods that improve with more computation can keep benefiting as computation becomes cheaper.
howItWorks: Start with a general method rather than specialist rules.
Give it more computation as resources grow.
Let performance improve through that added scale.
Compare long-run results, not only early performance.
explainer.whyItMatters: The lesson encourages AI researchers to favor approaches that can continue improving as computational resources grow. It also cautions against expecting short-term gains from specialist knowledge to remain decisive in the long run.
misconceptions: It does not say domain knowledge is always useless.
More computation does not guarantee better performance.
It concerns long-run tendencies, not every fixed budget.
